doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Recording plans and thematic albums; goodbye
summary: She plans albums as curves from beginning to end; interview ends.

story.theme_name: Thanks and goodbyes: closing the interview
story.community_name: Closing the interview: thanks, goodbyes and tape running out

blocks.x: All right. I’ll look forward to that. You have recording plans coming up?
Yeah. I think things will get underway I hope this spring yeah.
Is it hard for you to — let’s say you have a record date coming up and you’re able to do six of your own tunes. Is it hard for you to pick six? Do you have that much material of your own?
That you say I want to do all this?

There’s more than enough material to keep recording for a long, long time. That’s not a problem. That’s not a problem. It’s just when I make a record I like to think about recordings, like I said, in a special way. I like to think about how they make a statement from beginning to end. In the old days they used to call it kind of thematic albums, but even if there’s some you know kind of thread in my own mind, about some kind of concept I’m trying to get across, you know, in everything that this music states in an album, so it’s not just about cut, cut, cut you know. Here’s a song, here’s a song, here’s a song and we’re going to splice them together you know. I try to think about an album as a curve from beginning to end, and what connects it and what I’m trying to say with each statement. And hopefully that makes it the kind of album that you want to listen to not just once, but many times, and after five or ten or fifteen years it might be worth listening to again, if the values on it are strong enough.
All right. Well you have some things to do later on today, and —
— here on the campus and thank for your time and I’m sure we’ll be hearing some great things about you in the future.
